name: Laxogenin
lead: Laxogenin is a plant-derived steroidal sapogenin (3-beta-hydroxy-5-alpha-spirostan-6-one) first characterised from plants such as Allium chinense (the 'Xiebai' bulb of Chinese medicine) and Smilax sieboldii [1][2]. It is sold in bodybuilding supplements under claims of muscle-building, often described as a 'plant steroid'.

Published literature on laxogenin consists of phytochemistry, cell-culture and plant-growth work. One study of antitumour-promoting activity in cell assays and one analytical study identifying spirostanes in bodybuilding supplements exist [2][3]. No published human trial of laxogenin for muscle or appearance was found.

paras: Laxogenin is the aglycone of saponins such as xiebai-saponin I, isolated from the bulbs of Allium chinense, a traditional Chinese crude drug, and from Smilax sieboldii rhizomes [1][2]. Chemists have also used laxogenin as a starting material to synthesise saponins and brassinosteroid-type plant growth compounds [3][4].

In cell and in-vitro work, laxogenin and its glycosides were examined for antitumour-promoting activity and for effects on hypoxia-related tyrosine kinase signalling in endothelial cells [1][5]. A plant-science paper describes laxogenin C as a plant growth regulator [6]. These studies do not address muscle growth in humans.

Laxogenin appears in bodybuilding products, and a 2019 analytical chemistry paper describes methods for unequivocally identifying spirostanes in such supplements [7]. Proponents describe it as a plant-derived, non-hormonal anabolic; the sources reviewed here do not document a human mechanism.
No studies found. Related laboratory and plant research is limited to the cell and phytochemical work described above [1][5][6].

card.summary: Plant steroid-like saponin sold for muscle; research is lab and plant work only, no human trials.
card.note: No human safety or efficacy data found.

quick.overview:
Laxogenin is a compound from plants like Allium chinense, marketed to bodybuilders as a natural anabolic.

Its published research is chemistry, cell and plant work. No human trial was found.
quick.mechanism: No human mechanism for muscle growth has been published. Lab work covers cell assays and plant growth regulation.
quick.risks: No human safety data were found. Supplement contents can vary, and analytical studies have been needed to identify spirostanes in products.
